title: A Test Bed to Examine Helmet Fit and Retention and Biomechanical Measures of Head and Neck Injury in Simulated Impact
protocol: Define fit scenarios on an anthropometric test device head with a circumference of 575 mm.
Mark each helmet position on the headform for consistent repetition of fit scenarios.
Use a CPSC certified helmet, available in universal size, for all fit scenarios.
Tighten the chinstrap to leave approximately one finger width of space under the chin.
Hand-tighten the adjustable dial to maintain a secure fit.
Arrange five fit sensors on the skin of the headform positioned at front, back, left, right, and top.
Take a reference measurement with transducers on the un-helmeted headform under no load.
Place the helmet onto the headform and measure force data for 3 s at a rate of 2.5 kHz.
Repeat the fit scenario six times for repeated measurements.
Convert wavelength shift data to force measurements by multiplying measured wavelengths from the transducer by the pre-determined calibration constant.
Assemble a drop tower consisting of an adjustable drop gimbal, an anthropometric test device head and neck, and a variable impact surface.
Arrange 9 uni-axial accelerometers in a 3-2-2-2 configuration within the headform to determine linear and angular accelerations at the center of gravity.
Arrange a purpose-built velocity gate on the impact tower to measure impact velocity immediately before impact.
Collect head acceleration and neck force/moment data using the data acquisition system.
Filter analog voltages sampled at 100 kHz for all channels.
Include a hardware anti-aliasing low pass filter with a corner frequency of 4 kHz prior to the data acquisition system.
Arrange the impact scenario by removing the helmet visor for better visibility during motion tracking.
Arrange all drops to impact the forehead, as it is a common impact location in cycling.
Simulate six different impact scenarios by varying impact speed and surface type.
Raise the headform to the appropriate height corresponding to specified impact velocities of 4 m/s or 6 m/s.
Drop the headform from an appropriate height to achieve desired velocities, typically 0.82 m for 4 m/s and 1.83 m for 6 m/s.
Add height as necessary to overcome friction losses.
Arrange either a flat or a 45° angled anvil as the impact surface.
The flat anvil simulates falls on a flat surface.
The angled anvil simulates impacts with a tangential velocity component.
Cover both surfaces of the anvils with abrasive tape to simulate an asphalt surface.
Adjust the anvil position between impacts to ensure only the flat surface is contacted by the helmet being tested.
Arrange the drop tower configuration for either head-first or torso-first impact scenarios.
Simulate a head-first impact without adjusting the drop tower setup.
For torso-first impacts, place a wooden block at a height such that the head is approximately 25 mm away from impacting the anvil when the torso hits first.
Add a layer of foam to minimize vibrations from the drop tower.
Adjust the angle of the neck in torso-first impacts to allow for forehead impact after flexion.
Include side impacts scenarios by adjusting the setup accordingly.
Trigger the data acquisition system.
Activate high speed cameras.
Drop the headform simultaneously.
Repeat the same impact and fit scenario configuration 3 times with new helmets each time.
Subject each of the four fit scenarios to each of the 6 different impact scenarios.
Perform a total of 72 drops after 3 trials of each configuration.
Post-process the headform kinematic and kinetic data.
Filter analog signals for acceleration using a 4th order Butterworth filter.
Filter analog signals for force/moment using a 4th order Butterworth filter.
Filter head accelerations as per Channel Frequency Class (CFC) 1000.
Filter neck forces as per CFC 1000.
Filter neck moments as per CFC 600.
Arrange high-speed cameras around the drop tower.
Record marker positions from two high speed cameras.
Arrange two high-speed cameras around the drop tower to capture synchronized images of the helmet and headform movement during impact.
Place a master camera to the side of the drop tower and place a slave camera at approximately 45° from the master.
Set up a 250 W light between the cameras to allow for sufficient exposure.
Configure high speed cameras.
Equip each camera with either a 50 mm f/1.4 or 100 mm f/2.0 macro lens, depending on the field of view required.
Set the apertures on the lenses at f/8.0.
Configure both cameras to record at 1280 x 800 pixels at a frame rate of 1000 frames per second or faster.
Synchronize the two cameras in frames and internal clock.
Set up a trigger so that both cameras trigger simultaneously.
Calibrate the space by taking a still image of a calibration frame from each camera.
Move a calibration cage with 17 known calibration point locations into the field of view of both cameras and take a single image from each camera.
Place motion tracking markers on the headform.
Take a still reference image of the headform from each camera.
Ensure that the reference image consists of three markers and a reference marker defined on the head.
Maximize the distance between markers using three reference point locations while remaining in both cameras' field of views.
Hold the reference marker between the eyes on the lower forehead.
Place three additional markers across the headform.
Ensure that these three additional markers are visible from both cameras during an impact.
Place motion tracking markers on the helmet.
Take still reference images of the helmet from each camera as described for the headform reference.
Ensure that the reference consists of viewing at least four motion tracking markers.
Hold one marker on the bottom of the helmet brim as a reference.
Spread three additional markers across the helmet.
Ensure that these three markers are visible from both cameras during an impact.
Take a single image from each camera for the helmet reference.
Trigger the data acquisition system, high-speed cameras, and drop of the headform simultaneously.
Arrange the helmet fit scenario.
Record the drop.
Signal a trigger to the cameras manually upon impact.
Arrange recording so that 3 seconds is recorded prior to the trigger.
Arrange recording so that 8 seconds is recorded after the trigger.
Manually review and bracket the synchronized camera images to contain the impact only.
Track head and helmet markers throughout the impact using camera-specific software.
Track six points per drop: three on both the helmet and headform.
Determine the transient two-dimensional pixel coordinates of each marker using the software.
Use the DLT method to calculate three-dimensional coordinates of tracked markers during a drop.
Calculate the 3-D dimensional coordinates of the headform forehead and helmet brim using the SVD method.
Estimate the location of a reference point on each the headform forehead and helmet brim from the tracked markers using the SVD method.
Find the transformation matrix of the three markers between the reference frame and each individual frame of a drop using the SVD method.
Apply the transformation to find either the forehead or helmet brim locations for indirect tracking.
Monitor the displacement between the forehead and helmet brim.
